video_title: Why Tariffs Actually Make Sense with Michael Every (Rabobank Strategist)
gist: Rabobank global strategist Michael Every argues markets are misreading the US as chaotic when it is running deliberate economic statecraft — using tariffs, energy, military and foreign policy jointly to remain 'top dog' and re-industrialize on a pre-1945 template. He frames the failed US strike on Iran as an oil/supply-chain move that China neutralized by drawing down reserves, lays out three branching Iran scenarios with different market outcomes, and says Europe's core vulnerability is its own fragmentation as it drifts toward a China trade war and a choice between Washington and Beijing.

themes.theme: Economic statecraft vs. siloed economic policy

insights.claim: Michael Every distinguishes economic policy (a single technocratic lever aimed at a target inside one silo) from economic statecraft, where tax, monetary, fiscal, FX, energy, defense and transport policy are wielded together to gain national power in a zero-sum international environment.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Analysts modelling US actions as isolated policy shocks will systematically mis-forecast; the correct unit of analysis is the joined-up national-power objective behind them.
insights.quote: Economic statecraft is when you look at every single tool that you have as part of a toolkit which collectively can be used to gain national power in a zero sum international environment.

insights.claim: Apparent US policy chaos and bewilderment can be a deliberate instrument, and observers who only think in single-silo technocratic terms mistake method for madness.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Fading 'policy incoherence' headlines as noise may be the wrong reflex — the confusion itself can be part of the strategy and can persist rather than mean-revert.
insights.quote: they failed to see that sometimes the madness is actually the method

insights.claim: The defining question of economic statecraft is 'what is GDP for?' rather than whether GDP prints 2.1%, and Europe is only starting to ask fragments of that question.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Policy regimes that redefine GDP's purpose license actions (tariffs, capital controls, industrial subsidies) that conventional macro models treat as irrational and therefore under-price.
insights.quote: The question that you ask if you are using economic statecraft is what is GDP for?

themes.theme: US grand strategy: a return to the 19th-century playbook

insights.claim: The US grand strategy is to stay the world's top power while radically transforming its economy away from the model it has run for the 45 years since the end of the Cold War, toward something resembling 18th, 19th and early 20th century America.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Positions built on the post-Cold-War globalization regime persisting are exposed to a multi-decade structural regime change, not a one-term policy cycle.
insights.quote: it's to remain top dog globally, whilst at the same time radically transforming their economy away from the model that they've had for the past 45 years since the end of the cold war

insights.claim: Tariffs are historically the American norm and the tariff-free decades of recent history were the anomaly, so the current tariff wave is a return to normality rather than an aberration.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Betting on tariff repeal as a reversion to a 'normal' free-trade baseline misidentifies which regime is the anomaly; tariffs are more likely to persist across administrations.
insights.quote: The only era in which America didn't have significant tariffs were the last few decades.

insights.claim: The US is reviving a developmental state in which government acts like an investment bank to grow the private sector, alongside a Monroe-Doctrine-style hemispheric foreign policy nicknamed the 'Dunroe doctrine'.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Expect more state co-investment, subsidies and directed credit in US industry, and more US assertiveness in Latin America — both were signalled in advance and are still under-priced.

insights.claim: The US national security strategy openly targets six things at once — the world's largest economy, the most dynamic economy, the most powerful military, energy dominance, AI dominance, and re-industrialization to fund all of it — with execution quality varying sharply by area.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: This list is a published roadmap of where US subsidies, tariffs and regulatory relief will keep flowing; it also flags green tech as the deliberately excluded pillar.
insights.quote: They want to have the world's most powerful military. They want to have energy dominance and they want to dominate AI.

insights.claim: US energy policy and AI policy are deliberately joined: cheap electricity is treated as a precondition for AI leadership, which is why the administration is pushing energy costs down while abandoning green tech.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Watch US power prices as the binding constraint on the data-center buildout; policy support skews to conventional generation and away from green tech.
insights.quote: we want to be an AI power and have really expensive electricity. How does that work?

themes.theme: Iran war: three branching scenarios and their market payoffs

insights.claim: The US attacked Iran for three logical reasons — Iranian oil, control of the Middle Eastern energy complex, and building an India-to-Europe trade bridge via the Middle East that shuts China out — following the same commodity-supply-chain logic used in Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Frames Middle East risk as a contest over upstream commodity control rather than nuclear proliferation alone, which changes which assets (oil, shipping, corridor infrastructure) are the real exposures.
insights.quote: if Iran logically was the next target it would be because a it's oil b the Middle Eastern energy complex and c because the US wanted to try and build a trade bridge between India and Europe via the Middle East to shut China out of the loop.

insights.claim: Every assigns a slightly higher probability to renewed war with Iran than to either a permanent US climbdown or an Iranian pivot, expecting the current 60-day negotiations to roll into further fruitless rounds until after the US midterm elections.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Implies a post-midterms window of elevated oil and geopolitical risk that current calm negotiation headlines are not pricing.
insights.quote: I would say that the probability is slightly higher at the moment that war is the more logical option if Iran isn't going to budge.

insights.claim: A second round of US-Iran war would spook markets initially but then calm down, because Every believes it would not do the same damage the first round did given better preparation.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Argues for fading the initial risk-off spike on any renewed Iran conflict rather than chasing it.
insights.quote: markets will freak out initially, but then they'll probably calm down because I think it won't do the same damage second time round it did first time round.

insights.claim: The low-probability but transformative Iran scenario is a Venezuela-style flip in which Iran gives up uranium and Hezbollah in exchange for reintegration and a flood of GCC capital, producing a Middle East boom and materially lower energy prices.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A tail scenario that is structurally bearish oil and strongly bullish Middle East growth assets — cheap optionality precisely because it is dismissed as unlikely.
insights.quote: Energy prices will come down a lot and it's going to be good news for growth for, you know, tens if not hundreds of millions of people.

themes.theme: The US-China card game: rare earths vs. commodity chokepoints

insights.claim: China blunted the Iran oil shock by drawing down its huge strategic reserves and cutting oil imports massively, which kept the price spike far smaller than it would otherwise have been.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Chinese reserve policy is now a first-order suppressor of oil spikes — a variable oil bulls must track alongside OPEC and US shale.
insights.quote: China immediately started to dip into its huge reserves and dropped its oil imports massively, which actually made sure the crisis wasn't as big as it would otherwise have been.

insights.claim: The US-China contest is a repeated card game in which China holds rare earths, electrification and vast commodity reserves giving it six to nine months of staying power, while the US plays upstream control of commodity supply chains via Venezuela and Iran.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Frames the conflict as a sequence of hands rather than a single outcome — each round's loser plays again, so de-escalation headlines are rounds, not endings.
insights.quote: I've got electrification. I've got vast reserves. I can ride this out for six to nine months. You can't.

insights.claim: The US is delegating the Taiwan geopolitics file to Japan and the Philippines while keeping deal-making space open with Beijing, so Chinese pressure is being aimed at Tokyo and Manila rather than Washington directly.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Taiwan escalation risk shows up first in Japanese and Philippine assets and China-Japan trade measures, not in direct US-China confrontation headlines.
insights.quote: the US, if anything, is actually delegating the geopolitics file on Taiwan to Japan and the Philippines supporting it.

insights.claim: Regional flashpoints should not be modelled in isolation: a single grand bargain spanning Taiwan, Russia-Ukraine and the Middle East is more likely than separate regional deals.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Cross-region correlation is higher than consensus assumes — a breakthrough or breakdown in one theatre should be traded across all of them.
insights.quote: you're more likely to get one big deal with everybody than you are to get individual deals in one particular region.

themes.theme: Europe's fragmentation and the coming EU-China trade war

insights.claim: Europe's single biggest strategic vulnerability is that Europe does not function as Europe — it speaks with one voice while remaining many smaller parts that are not greater than their sum, each too small to compete at global scale.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Structural discount on European assets versus US and Chinese scale persists until governance consolidates; headline EU 'strategy' announcements should be discounted for delivery risk.
insights.quote: Biggest vulnerability of Europe is Europe. The fact that Europe isn't Europe.

insights.claim: Europe is on the cusp of a deep trade war with China that will be as transformative for Europe as the US-China conflict was for the US — while European narrative still mocks Trump's tariffs as pointless, and Europe faces a far stronger China than Trump first confronted.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: An under-discussed catalyst: EU-China tariff escalation would hit European industrial supply chains and Chinese export names, and is being ignored precisely because it contradicts Europe's free-trade self-image.
insights.quote: Europe is, if you read some of the headlines, right on the cusp of entering into a deep trade war with China, which will be every bit as transformative for Europe as it has been for the US versus China.

insights.claim: Genuine European strategic autonomy would require hitting supply chains, energy, industry, scale, military tech and fiscal rules simultaneously, and would mean walking away from both America and China — turning both into rivals at once.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Strategic autonomy is far more costly than European rhetoric implies, so the realistic path is alignment — capital should price partial, compromised autonomy, not the full version.
insights.quote: if Europe does do that you are effectively walking away from both America and China

insights.claim: Every observes Europe's drift is gradually toward working with the US against China, which forces Europe to give up ambitions like independent tech autonomy and its own stablecoin outside the US dollar loop.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Bearish for European digital-sovereignty and euro-stablecoin projects; supportive of continued dollar-denominated payment rails.
insights.quote: How do you work with the US against China and have tech autonomy?

insights.claim: Europe built an effective architecture for a world that no longer exists — a soft-power, rules-based, free-trade order — while actually running mercantilism dressed up in technocracy, importing as little and exporting as much as possible.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: In a world where every bloc wants to be the net exporter, Europe's surplus model has no counterparty — implying persistent pressure on European industrial earnings and the euro's trade channel.
insights.quote: always talks about free trade while importing as little as possible and exporting as much as possible, which actually is mercantalism, but Europe always dresses it up as free trade

insights.claim: Roughly 10,000 industrial jobs a month are disappearing in Germany as a direct product of other countries' industrial and trade policy that Europe has been unable to answer.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A running measure of European deindustrialization; continued deterioration raises the odds of the EU-China tariff response Every expects.
insights.quote: I believe 10,000 jobs a month are disappearing in Germany, for example, in the industrial sector.

themes.theme: Tariff mechanics: when they work and when they don't

insights.claim: US tariffs so far show mixed results: no broad-based industrial revival yet, with input costs being pushed higher partly by the Iran war and partly by the initial impact of the tariffs themselves.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Near-term the tariff trade is a margin-squeeze story for input-heavy manufacturers, not yet a reshoring earnings story.
insights.quote: You haven't seen this broad-based industrial revival yet. You are seeing input costs being pushed higher partly by the Iran war, but partly by the initial impact of tariffs.

insights.claim: Because the US has its own raw materials such as copper, it cannot copy the East Asian model of tariffing only finished goods — it must tariff cheap inputs too, which makes everything more expensive in the near term.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Predicts upstream US commodity tariffs (copper and other inputs) as a policy necessity, supporting domestic raw-material producers and squeezing downstream manufacturers.
insights.quote: So, ironically, they have to tariff cheap inputs as well as cheap finished products.

insights.claim: Tariffs done right are only temporarily inflationary and then trigger a deflationary supply-side response that no mainstream model assumes; tariffs done wrong are simply inflationary — the difference is whether they are paired with the right subsidies and domestic purchasing power.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: If correct, consensus inflation forecasts that treat tariffs as permanently inflationary overstate the medium-term price path and understate the industrial capex response.
insights.quote: You can do tariffs wrong and they're inflationary. You can do tariffs right and they're temporarily inflationary and then actually you get a supply side response which no mainstream model ever assumes.

insights.claim: China, Japan and historically the US all built manufacturing superpower status behind heavy tariffs and non-tariff barriers, so tariff-led industrialization is observable history rather than voodoo economics — but it plays out over far longer than 18 months.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Sets the correct evaluation horizon for the US tariff experiment — judging it on 18-month data will produce false negatives.
insights.quote: It's observable history. It just doesn't happen in 18 months.

themes.theme: The dollar-military-industry loop and mis-taught trade theory

insights.claim: The rules-based order rests on a closed and self-destroying loop: the dollar is backed by the US military, the military is backed by US industry, and US industry is destroyed by the global dollar system because everyone wants to hold US assets rather than US goods.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Implies structural policy pressure to weaken the dollar's global role and rebalance toward goods demand — the strategic case behind tariffs and capital-flow interventions.
insights.quote: the global dollar system means the dollar is too strong, which means US industry is too weak because everyone wants to hold US assets, not US goods.

insights.claim: What the US is doing messily is reconstructing an older, less utopian and more selfish system that narrows the imbalances the current system inevitably produces — and re-industrializing to shrink the US trade deficit will devastate the countries that export to it.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The identifiable losers are persistent surplus exporters; the transition, not the endpoint, is where the market damage concentrates.
insights.quote: If the US is going to re-industrialize and narrow its trade deficit, it will devastate people who export to it.

insights.claim: Ricardo's comparative advantage breaks down under mobile global capital — Ricardo himself said capital would simply relocate to the low-cost country and make both goods — and that part is edited out of how economics is taught because it contradicts free-market orthodoxy.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Removes the theoretical foundation for the assumption that tariffs are always welfare-destroying, which is the intellectual basis of consensus anti-tariff positioning.
insights.quote: Ricardo himself argued the system doesn't work like that if you have global capital, mobile global capital.

insights.claim: Sustained fundamental imbalances produce more inequality, more debt, more anger, more populism and eventually more wars until the system crumbles — a conclusion reached from Austrian, Marxist and anarchist starting points alike.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: Treats populism and conflict as endogenous outputs of the trade/financial architecture, so political risk should be modelled as a function of imbalance levels rather than as random shocks.
insights.quote: more and more unhappiness, more and more anger, more and more populism, more and more wars eventually and the whole system starts to crumble.

insights.claim: National resilience is itself zero-sum: a resilient economy saves more than it consumes, which means running a net export surplus, which forces a deficit onto someone else — so there is no universal path to resilience without collaboration.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: The global rush to 'resilience' and reshoring is mathematically a fight over who absorbs the deficit — expect escalating trade conflict, not convergence.
insights.quote: If you're resilient, that means that you have spare saving, which means you're not consuming everything that you produce, which is sensible, but that means you run a net export surplus.

insights.claim: Every names free trade as the most overrated idea in economics, noting most of human history had no free trade, and names conflating simultaneous crises in the Middle East, eastern Europe and Asia as the most underrated geopolitical risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Every
insights.so_what: A three-theatre simultaneous crisis is the tail scenario he flags as hardest to reverse — a correlation-blowout risk most geopolitical risk models treat as independent events.
insights.quote: There are so many, but I'll go for free trade. Free trade. Most of human history didn't have free trade.
